Eggs of the Humboldt penguin (Spheniscus humboldti) are typically incubated in burrows along the coast of Peru and Chile, where the thermal environment within the nest chamber is closely regulated by the attending adults. During this critical developmental period, the average incubation temperature is sustained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], which is somewhat lower than the species' core body temperature. The incubation period culminates in hatching after approximately 40 days [ab = approximately 40 days], a duration that is comparable to that of other medium-sized spheniscids at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Upon emergence, the hatchling is altricial and entirely dependent on parental provisioning. The first body mass measurement recorded shortly after the chick has dried reveals a wet weight at birth of 96 grams [Wwb = 96 grams], which represents a modest fraction of the ultimate adult mass. This small initial size places a high demand on the parents, who must deliver nutrients frequently to sustain the rapid growth trajectory that characterizes the nestling phase.

During the nestling period, chicks grow rapidly, fed on regurgitated fish and krill by both parents. Within a few weeks, the pin-feathered chick begins to develop its downy insulation and becomes more active, though it remains confined to the nest burrow. At the core body temperature characteristic of incubation and brooding activity in this species, 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C], several key developmental milestones are achieved. Fledging, defined as the age at which the chick achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at 65 days after hatching [tx = 65 days after hatching] at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This timing is relatively early compared to congeneric species such as the African penguin Spheniscus demersus, in which the fledging period can extend from 60 to 100 days. The relatively short nestling phase in Humboldt penguins may be an adaptation to the variable marine productivity of the Humboldt Current, encouraging an early transition to independent foraging.

Longitudinal studies of marked individuals have provided valuable insights into the life history trajectory of this species under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolism in adult penguins. The attainment of sexual maturity, marked by the onset of gonadal activity and readiness to breed, is recorded at 195 days after birth [tp = 195 days after birth] at 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. This represents a relatively early puberty for a seabird of this body size. However, the onset of maturity does not immediately translate into successful reproduction, as first-time breeders often exhibit lower fledging success than more experienced pairs. The first successful brood, defined as the time since birth at which a pair produces its first clutch that yields fledglings, is typically deferred until approximately 730 days after birth [tR = approximately 730 days after birth], reflecting the time needed for territory acquisition, pair bonding, and development of foraging proficiency at a temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C].

Longevity records for Humboldt penguins in the wild and in captivity indicate a maximum lifespan of up to 27.3 years [am = up to 27.3 years] under optimal conditions, a value that aligns closely with estimates for the closely related Spheniscus demersus measured at the species' active metabolic temperature of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C]. As adults, individuals reach a maximum body mass that varies considerably across populations and sexes. While the range typically spans from 3.6 to 5.9 kilograms, repeated measurements of large, healthy adult males in well-studied colonies have documented an ultimate wet weight of 5,000 grams [Wwi = 5,000 grams], a value that is consistent with the species' position as a moderately sized penguin. Adult body condition fluctuates markedly over the annual cycle, with pre-molt individuals accumulating substantial lipid stores to sustain the fast associated with feather replacement.

Under the same thermal regime of 38.2 °C [T = 38.2 °C] that governs many of the species' physiological rates, the maximum reproductive output of the Humboldt penguin has been quantified. Females typically produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], which is the standard clutch size across the Spheniscus genus, and they can raise up to one successful clutch per year [F_R_i = up to one successful clutch per year]. This reproductive schedule is constrained by the lengthy chick-rearing period and the need for both adults to undergo a complete molt before the next breeding attempt. A comprehensive comparative analysis of the entire life cycle of Spheniscus humboldti reveals a suite of traits—rapid chick growth, early fledging, moderate adult body mass, and a deferred start to first successful breeding—that together reflect the species' adaptation to the cold, productive but unpredictable waters of its eastern Pacific range.
